utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Monday, September 14th, 2009, and I greet everyone in the courtroom, our accused, the Defence counsels, I also greet Mr. Scott and his case manager, as well as everyone helping us. I will first render a new oral decision, and I will read it slowly. Oral decision on the Prosecution's oral motion to review the decision pertaining to the Prosecution's request to re-consider the orders dealing with the cross-examination of expert witnesses Josip Jurcevic and Vlado Sakic. During the hearing of September 10th, 2009, the Prosecution made an oral motion to review the oral decision dealing with the Prosecution's motion pertaining to the cross-examination of expert witnesses Josip Jurcevic and Vlado Sakic issued on September 10th, 2009. The Trial Chamber reminds the Prosecution that it ruled on the time allotted to parties as far as cross-examination of these two expert witnesses concerned in its two orders dealing with the way these expert witnesses were to be heard, expert witnesses called Josip Jurcevic and Vlado Sakic; and the orders were dated April 22nd, 2009 and May 6th, 2009 and the Trial Chamber also ruled on this in its decision of September 10th, 2009. The Trial Chamber considers that the Prosecution's oral motion of September 10th, 2009, because of its form falls outside the Rules of Procedure and Evidence -- actually, the Prosecution should have filed a request for certification regarding the oral decision of September 10th according to Rule 73(C), if it had wished to do so. The Trial Chamber also wishes to underline once again that the Prosecution was extremely late in requesting for the orders to be reviewed and considers, thus, that this reflects a certain lack of diligence from the Prosecution in the way it dealt with the expert witnesses' report. Therefore, the Trial Chamber decides to reject the Prosecution's request. Mr. Kovacic, I believe that you wanted to take the floor but on something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Thank you, Your Honour, for giving me the floor. I have a very brief submission to make, and with our permission, I would like to submit a motion, or rather, to make a request to allow us approximately a maximum of 200 pages, additional 200 pages, to the 3.000-page limit for -- I'm sorry, I meant to say 200 words, not 200 pages. I'm sorry. I misspoke there. Well, we're off to a good start it seems today. Anyway, 200 words over the 3.000 limit. And it is a submission pursuant to Article 92 bis, which we have completed, and when we were working on the draft, final draft, yesterday and the day before we saw that we had some 3.200 words, actually a little over that, but we managed to cut it down to that number and my associates are working now to do the best we can. But we feel that 3.200 words would be sufficient for us to set out our arguments and I think we have all -- every reason to ask for those extra 200 words. So with your permission we can complete the task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me consult with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber has deliberated on this and is granting this motion. You can, therefore, use 3.200 words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me now ask our usher to come -- and go get the expert witness. Mr. Kovacic, how long is this examination-in-chief going to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as we've already stated, according to our schedule, I have envisaged an hour and 20 minutes, and I will adhere to that strictly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. If you can hear me in your own language, could you please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I can hear you and I can follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell us your name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Josip Jurcevic, the 19th of April, 1951, that's when I was born.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your job at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a Ph.D., a doctor of science.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where do you work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the Institute for Social Sciences called Ivo Pila Pilar in Zagreb, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you tell us whether you've already been in a witness in a trial regarding events that occurred in former Yugoslavia or whether this is the first time that you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was an expert witness at a trial in Vukovar in 1999, 1999/2000, and that was related to the aggression on the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell us whether you were a Court witness, a Prosecution witness, or a Defence witness as far as this trial -- that trial is concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court in Vukovar sent -- sent instructions to my institute that they should state their scholarly views with respect to the events in the former Yugoslavia, with respect to Vukovar and Croatia. And as I deal in matters of that kind, the institute assigned me to compile an expert report at the request of the Trial Chamber there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you testified, were you questioned by the Judges, the Prosecutor, and the counsels for Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After writing my written report, I did testify orally during the proceedings, and I was questioned by the Judges, the Prosecutor, and the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you please read the statement that is on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You can sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me give you some details. You are an expert witness called by the Defence of General Praljak. General Praljak asked you to come to provide your own contribution to the establishment of the truth. Contrary to what you told us when -- as far as what happened when you testified in -- for the Vukovar case, you are -- you've been called by one party only. So you're not a Court witness but you're a Defence witness. However, since you've just made the solemn declaration, you are now under oath and you are a witness of justice. If up until now you were in contact with the Defence of General Praljak, let me tell you that as of now you will no longer be in contact with them, notably since you're supposed to be heard from for several days. So let me remind you that you're not supposed to contact the Defence anymore. And the Trial Chamber is also asking you not to contact the media, to give them information on the questions or answers that you might provide or that you might -- or the answer that you might give in response to questions put to you by the Judges, by Mr. Kovacic, or by Mr. Scott. The Trial Chamber has your report. We've all studied it carefully, so we're not opening a blank page. The trial Judges have -- know about your report and because of this we might decide to ask a few questions. At one point in time if we want to save time or if we believe at one point in time you're going astray and you're not focusing enough, we might tell you to make shorter answers and to get back on track. For example, in your report you're talking about the co-operation between Croatians and Muslims. Let me tell you, we've heard a huge amount of evidence regarding this, so it's pointless to give us any examples of this because we've heard ample evidence on the subject. However, if you want to develop this topic but from another angle, you may do so. You know that the Trial Chamber is always controlling the way the witness is heard. Please try and be very specific in your answers. We're not here to lecture. We want you to answer the questions put to you very specifically. If you believe that the question is too ambiguous, or if it's not well formulated, please ask the person putting it, even if it's a Judge, to reformulate it. Nobody's perfect, of course. So if you believe that the question is not properly put, ask the person putting it to you to reformulate it. First you will be questioned by Mr. Kovacic. I'm sure that you've already met with him during the proofing session. Then once he'll be done, the other counsels will also ask questions if they want to; and then the Prosecutor, who's on your right, Mr. Scott, will then take the floor and put questions to you for cross-examination purposes. The three Judges in front of you on the Bench -- normally there's four of us, but, unfortunately, one of us is away today - might ask questions if we believe we need to. We'll see how the hearing unfolds anyway. There are 20-minute breaks every hour and 30 minutes, for two reasons, first so the witness can rest and also to change the tapes. If at any point in time you don't feel well, you feel ill at ease, just raise your hand and we can have a break. The Trial Chamber remains at your disposal, of course. Finally, let me remind you of a point that is very dear to the heart of my fellow Judge, Judge Prandler. Since you're speaking the same language as the counsel putting questions to you, please wait for the counsel to be done with his question before answering, otherwise you'll overlap and the court reporter will be unable to make the transcript because when we're talking and everything is translated into English and then everything is transcribed also. And in order to make sure that a transcript can be done, please make sure that there is -- that you don't answer too quickly. Wait for the question to be put to you before you answer. Sometimes the witness gets all -- is too fast. So you're an academic, so please keep in mind the fact that we're -- we're working in several languages and interpretation is difficult. It's not always completely comprehensive. But if we overlap, if we speak too fast, then the interpretation becomes even more complicated. And to -- and some information gets lost in the translation. So sometimes even I do so, sometimes I speak too fast. But, please, if you stick to these principles, the hearing should run smoothly. Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor Jurcevic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'd like to start off by asking you some introductory questions from your curriculum vitae, including the chapter -- well, we've provided all this to everybody on your education, scholarly work, and so on. You've already told us where and when you were born, but my first question is this: When did you graduate?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: I graduated in 1975, and I received my doctorate in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And which faculty did you graduate at?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The Faculty of Philosophy in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's microphones kindly be adjusted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What course? What department?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The history of philosophy -- or rather, history and philosophy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, at the same time or later on, study at other faculties as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, both parallelly and subsequently. I studied at a number of faculties, including two years of law, two years of economics, three years of political sciences. I graduated in the subject of the study of Marxism and the theory and practice of self-management socialism. I studied informatics for six semesters, two semesters of lay theology. I think that I have remembered them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll probably come to that later on, but I think that this is a good moment to ask you this: Why, Doctor, after graduating and while you were studying history and philosophy in actual fact, why did you go to study at other faculties? Why was this necessary to you as a historian? Why did you feel it necessary to do that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: I intended to work in research, research into modern history, and you can't do that if you only have classical training and education in history in view of the methodological complexity and the complexity of events in modern times, where different levels of knowledge intertwine, it is necessary to have a knowledge of the basics, the basics of methodology and other social sciences, in order to be able as objectively as possible to enter into a causal study of modern history.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, just to make sure that I've understood your answer, is that because method and methodology in modern historical terms requires interdisciplinary -- an interdisciplinary approach and a multidisciplinary approach; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For one objectively to understand modern happenings and events, you have to have a multi disciplinary and interdisciplinary approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after graduating you went on to do your MA and Ph.D., your doctoral and master's, thesis. Could you just tell us your topics in 1996 when you wrote your master's thesis and the year 2000 when you did your doctoral thesis. I hope I've got it right.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you have got it right. I received my MA degree on the topic of the problems of studying the victims of World War II in the territory of Croatia, and my doctoral thesis was the -- the dissertation was the repressiveness of the Yugoslav system in Croatia in 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also provided us with your scholarly research work and your teaching efforts, and we have this on page 4, 9 of your curriculum vitae. And from that, let me ask you this: Is it true that you took part in a number of scientific research projects, either as project leader or member of the team, and did you also take part in a series of lectures and did you teach; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was project leader for a whole series of projects, and I took part as a researcher on many projects related to the latest or modern-day history. Similarly, apart from working in the institute, I teach at several universities. I teach modern world history and modern national, Croatian, history.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: And also I teach a Ph.D. course on those same topics and that includes the methodology on modern sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you attached to your expert report - and we have provided that to everybody here - a list of your writings included -- including your books, text books, scholarly reports, et cetera, your work in editorial -- in the editorial field and even documentaries. So for those who would like to follow, I'm referring to pages 10 to 17 of the curriculum vitae and its attachments. Could you now just tell us in a word what the main topics of the works you've published were. What were the issues you dealt with most?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The focus of my attention in my scholarly work was on three basic topics: The first being the Croatian homeland war; the second, the war and post-war suffering linked to World War II; and third, research into the Croatian emigres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to ask you two questions with respect to the methodology and standards applied to the elaboration of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I have a question. You said that you published a number of documents. You published one in 1998, The Origins of the Myth of Jasenovac. Can you tell us what you were trying to demonstrate in this book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That book on Jasenovac -- well, that was the title given for publishing reasons, it was actually my master's thesis, which I wrote in 1996 and defended at the faculty of philosophy in Zagreb. And in the briefest of terms, it is -- I deal with the fact that there was manipulation by the communist system into the victims of World War II in order to achieve certain political and other goals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So in relation to the standard and the methodology you used when you wrote your thesis -- actually, I have a question in relation to that. Could you tell me what the standards you applied were with regard to this expert report. You do refer to that in the introduction, but I would appreciate an explanation here and now.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the expert report was drafted on the basis of methodological standards applied in modern science. The aim of the expert report was to portray in a causal sense, that is to say the causes, the actual developments and the consequences of what was being researched, that is to say what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina until 1995, from 1991 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Doctor, everyone who does this kind of work ultimately has his or her own feeling deep down in their hearts as to what the results of their work actually were like. This is not exactly customary, but I'm going to ask you something. You wrote this expert report. You looked at a great many questions. Are you personally satisfied on the whole with the result of your labours?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am very satisfied with what I did, if I may say, quite immodestly. I believe that so far this is the one and only piece of writing devoted to this particular topic that had a comprehensive approach, and that is explained in greater detail in the introduction and in various chapters in the report itself. That means that this expert report was primarily based on facts. What can clearly be seen is what the level of the expert report was, and also various propositions that were made in this expert report can be checked easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have just one more question while we're still on the subject -- or rather, the introduction to your report, page 5 in Croatian, page 5 in English. Did you have any specific problems? Did you have any specific requests when you were dealing with the subject?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were quite a few problems involved. I'll refer to the two basic ones that are untypical. One is the problem of sources. Since the institutions of the Republic of Croatia -- or rather, the institutions in Bosnia-Herzegovina have not really put their archives in order to this day and that takes up a great deal of time and makes research increasingly difficult. The second problem was the fact that in public life, through the media, in the political sphere, et cetera, because of different interests involved in the public, there are different stereotypes, or rather, misconceptions regarding reality; namely, the causes of what had happened and the actual developments that took place, not even to mention the interpretations of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am going to move on to the expert report itself now. If you have any questions in relation to what we've dealt with so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall call you "Professor" since you are teaching in a number of places. I looked very carefully at all the books you have written and all the articles you co-authored. There's one or two that caught my attention. I think you prefaced the book which Mr. Praljak wrote on the fall of the old bridge. And you seemingly also wrote in 2006 an article on the activity of this Tribunal, and you mentioned this concept of joint criminal enterprise with the question mark: What is it? Could you tell me, please, what you based your article on. To assess the activities of this Tribunal, what did you read, the judgements or a number of other documents? What exactly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, it is correct that I wrote the preface to the book, "How the Old Bridge was Destroyed." This is a compilation of documents and I was the editor too. Second question, yes, it is true that I wrote that article. Before that, I spoke at a symposium in Zagreb in relation to this topic. Several experts participated in this symposium, people from different lines of work, both from Croatia and other European countries. My topic was the historical and political aspects of the activity of The Hague Tribunal. From the point of view of modern historical science, I compared some of the fundamental postulates involved since the inception of The Hague Tribunal, its public activity in particular especially of the OTP, and I compare that to international legal standards and experiences of the most important world court in the 20th century. There weren't any before that in actual fact. And the most important world court in the 20th century were the Nuremberg Tribunals. The point was not to go into the legal aspect of the matter, but to assess the public impact in view of the interest of the international entities involved, particularly different courts. In particular, it was to send a message out loud and clear that crime does not pay off. I explained that in the introduction and in the conclusion, and I said that it was necessary in these global conditions of the world the fact that there is such a great degree of permeation of different factors. I said that it was indispensable to have an international judiciary at a comprehensive level. Just like at national level, in every country, there is an overall judiciary and, therefore, there should be an international judiciary, and they should have appropriate powers so as to be effective and efficient. That is what I wrote there. And another thing that I wrote was that it was exceptionally important to deal with all the difficulties involved in the building of the international judiciary. This makes the responsibility of current international courts even greater among the public, especially those who make decisions regarding the establishment of international courts, but also it goes beyond that. Utmost attention should be devoted to these matters. Steps should be taken carefully because all of this will be only -- enhanced even further. I can speak at even greater length, Your Honours, but this is it in a nutshell. I am an advocate of having an international judiciary because this is what the required in the situation in the world on the whole, especially because the 20th century was a century in which unspeakable crimes happened and this happened at an international level. However, in most cases, all these crimes were not prosecuted or sanctions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you were born on the 19th of April, 1951, in this small village of Studenci where you seemingly wrote a small article on the life in this village. In 1991 and 1992, you were 40. Did you do your military service? Did you volunteer? Were you called up when the conflict broke out? And if you did, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In relation to the period between 1990 and 1995, I was a volunteer in the Croatian homeland war, from the spring of 1991 up until the summer of 1992. I was one of the founders and commanders of a volunteer unit that was called the platoon for documentary and informational activity. The unit consisted of different experts, historians, historians of art, directors, journalists, et cetera, and the point was to collect material about everything that was going on, written records, audio records, video records, visual records, 3D, so on and so forth. We preserved all of this. There were many exhibitions that were staged, many films were made. Likewise, I tried to establish a central archive for the Ministry of Defence. In a way, this is a paradox. I left the army precisely because of the archives, and in my discharge papers, it says that I was one of the founders of the central archive of the Ministry of Defence. It hadn't been established formally yet and it is due to that fact that I left the HVO, or rather, the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, inter alia, in your publications there is a contribution which is entitled: "The Geneva Conventions and the Experience of Camp Detainees." Now, I'm not asking you to resume the article. What I would like to know is what detainees did this deal with? Croatian? Serbian? Muslim? Separate? Together? If you could answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was an article and an accurate answer to your question would be the following: I do not make any kind of discriminatory distinction on any basis. As for the experience of camp inmates, our source for this were reports of different international organisations, including the expert report from 1995 regarding camps. This could be obtained on the internet as well. Also I compared international law and the Geneva Conventions on the one hand and the protection of all victims in camps on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Looking at your list of publications, I got the impression that Croats and Croatia only appear as victims. Is it a correct impression, that you have never done any research into the allegations that one can hear of crimes and atrocities coming from Croatians in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No -- or rather, as you can see from the list of my work, I do not engage in any kind of discrimination. I do not emphasise Croatian in any sense. For example, with regard to my Ph.D., I referred to all the inhabitants of Croatia regardless of their ethnic background, their gender, their origins in any way. As is customary in the Western world when one says the "French," the "Americans," any other term denoting the citizens of a state. That is what is meant in Croatia too. What is primarily meant are citizens of Croatia. Now that you've asked this question, I would like to say in many of my speeches and works, I advocated the rights of national minorities in different ways, socially and from the point of view of the war that was going on and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You go beyond the strict answer to the question. I just want to make one thing sure. I was -- clear. I was certainly not accusing you of discrimination at all, and I know very well that a scientist is free in picking the subject that he wants to study. But I have not heard you say that you have studied specifically, let us say, dark sides of Croatian history where Croatia was rather the problematic actor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're referring to the period of the Second World War, I wrote articles about that as well. I stated very clearly what it was all about. I was saying that this was a criminal system, totalitarian, asocial, that the worst types of crimes were committed. When speaking of the Republic of Croatia where I live, I am one of the most prominent scholars who criticised very sharply many bad things in the Republic of Croatia, both from a social point of view and from a scientific point of view, and any other point of view for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I would like to seek a clarification from you. You told us that you volunteered, that you commanded a volunteers' unit which was designed to collect information, videos. I assume this unit reported to the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, ultimately in formal terms that unit was responsible to the Ministry of Defence, reported to the Ministry of Defence; but up until I left the military, it was truly a unit of volunteers, or rather, most of the equipment, most of the cassettes, most of -- all the things that were needed for production, for preservation, et cetera, all of that was dealt with by the actual members of the unit. Everything that was done depended on the goodwill of the members of that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you leave this unit, on what date exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at that time, I was already in the Ministry of Defence, one of the founders of the department for information and psychological operations, and I was the director of something that did not exist in the actual fact but formally did exist and that was the archive. And I left in early July 1992. I and almost the entire unit because we were unhappy with the status and how the archive was actually treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In August 1992, in September, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was unemployed up until the very end of 1994 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until July 1992, you were in charge of this unit, and then you were in charge of the setting up of the archives. Did you have the opportunity to meet General Praljak at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the spring of 1992, that was the first time when I physically met him personally. We had some kind of a superficial communication. At that time, he was the assistant minister and he covered the department where I was. He was in charge of that too. And I can say that in this hierarchy there was some misunderstanding for a number of reasons - I'm not going to go into that - or lack of understanding about the importance of the archive. And that is why I believe that the whole hierarchy superior to me, including General Praljak either directly or indirectly, in a way caused my departure from the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You partly answered the question I was about to put to you. In the spring of 1992 General Praljak is in hierarchical terms above you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the hierarchy, as I've just explained to you, giving you an example, did not really mean much in light of the general disorder in the Croatian institutions at the time, including the army and the defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In political terms, did you belong to any political party or were you not affiliated to any party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the second Yugoslavia, I was not a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and after 1990, I did not enroll in any party. I am not a member of any party to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw that you have seven children. Does your wife work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am a father of seven. All seven still live in the same household with me. My wife has a Ph.D. from the Bremen University in Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your wife who has a Ph.D. in science, is she practicing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, she works in the same institute where I, myself, work. That's where we met before we actually got together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question because I could spend hours putting questions to you, as you may well imagine. But I do not -- I don't wish to be tedious vis-a-vis my audience. In this period, between 1992 and 1994 as part of this volunteers' unit, did you ever go in the field to Bosnia-Herzegovina or did you never go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went to Bosnia-Herzegovina several times, not on anyone's behest or order. I went there on my own initiative and members of my unit did the same. The main purpose was to gather as much material as we could on the ground and to encounter persons who were also gathering materials as volunteers and establish co-operation with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't going to put anymore questions, but I must put you a question now. You said that you went to Bosnia-Herzegovina. You went there on the ground. And you and your colleagues, you collected information. What was your status at the time? You were a military, weren't you, when you went to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult to explain the time and the situation to somebody who lives in an order, state, or society when institutions and, indeed, everything else function well. At the time very, few things did function, both in the Republic of Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in particular in the latter. So it was possible to just enter Bosnia and Herzegovina at any point, and also the other way round. That means -- if you're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were there, were you working there as a civilian? Weren't you, in fact, in charge of gathering data for the intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never. In my entire life I never engaged in any intelligence activity, and I know very well from my scientific research what intelligence work entails. Several members of my unit were originally from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Sometimes I went there to visit them because they had gone to Bosnia and Herzegovina as volunteers, and the primary interest of all of us was to gather materials, video materials, documents, and so on, about what was going on. So that I did not go to Bosnia and Herzegovina as an official. Only on one occasion, I think it was in May 1992, did I actually go to Posavina in my official capacity, since the chief of the department where I worked - and it was not clear what was going on there - I and some other people went there simply to see what was going on in co-operation with the HVO members from that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question: When you went to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you meet General Praljak on the ground there or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a very short question which calls for a very short answer. You have told us that the hierarchy was somewhat not very clear, but still perhaps you can say how many steps were between Mr. Praljak and you in that department where you both were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked in the department which was called the department for information and psychological operations. It was headed by the chief, and General Praljak was one of the several assistant ministers, and he was covering my department and a number of other departments -- well, in accordance with the structure of the ministry at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The short answer would have been: There was no in between. He was your direct superior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Between us there was at least a chief of the department for information and psychological operations. So there was at least one person between us, formally speaking, in hierarchical terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question regarding your resume. I noted that in the previous documentation we have pages of them and it's quite interesting, but you quoted Charles Shrader. Did you ever meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I am aware, I have never met him. I've never spoken to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, in your expert report, in compliance with our instructions, you started with the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina up until the break-up of the second Yugoslavia. If we look at the contents at the beginning of the analysis, that's chapter 1, and you can see that it covers 58 pages in the Croatian language. But I would first like to ask you a general question and then we will deal with a short excerpt from that chapter. So my general question about this chapter that deals with the recent history of Bosnia-Herzegovina up until the break-up of the SFRY. Do you stand by everything that you wrote in terms of sources and the contents and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: I stand by what I wrote in that part and in every part of my expert report, and the standards as to the foundations of all that are quite clearly stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will not go into that chapter at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions for you at the beginning, Professor, regarding the last part of the chapter that is entitled: "The break-up of the institutional system of the second Yugoslavia in the period of 1990 to 1992." It's at page 53 in the Croatian text and those who follow the English version, that's at page 46. Let me now try just ask you a few questions to sum up this chapter. So first question, could you please just answer yes or no if you can. Before the break-up of the SFRY, so before 1990/1991, was the League of Communists of Yugoslavia a relevant, cohesive factor in the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The League of Communists of Yugoslavia was the only key factor since it covered all the institutions in the state and social system in Yugoslavia. All the other political organisations were, in fact, banned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And now when we came to the time when the second Yugoslavia, the system of it broke down, what was the watershed in the history of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, the SKJ?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: In January 1990, there was the 14th extraordinary congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, where the League of Communists of Yugoslavia ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, I would like to interrupt you, sir. That's at page 48 in the English version. I think it's the third paragraph on that page. So please go ahead, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: That was the key incident in the break-up of the second Yugoslavia, and this belief that this is the key event that the break-up of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia necessarily entailed the break-up of the SFRY was first broached immediately in the aftermath of the congress in a number of analyses that appeared in the media and in scientific papers in the former Yugoslavia. It is particularly obvious now when you look at it from a certain temporal distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: After the formal break-up of the SKJ, did the multi-party system finally evolve or did it actually emerge at an earlier date?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The multi-party system in the former Yugoslavia began in a variety of ways in different republics. And one could say that in most of the republics some semi-legal forms of forming of parties started as early as in 1989. For instance, in mid-1989, in May, first the -- the first party was formed, and it was registered, but it was a semi-legal establishment or formation, that was the Croatian Social Liberal Alliance. And then in June in weird circumstances, if I may say that, the Croatian Democratic Union was formed, and it actually won the first multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When did the first multi-party elections take place after the new political parties were formed in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The first multi-party elections in Croatia were held in two rounds. The first round was in mid-April, and the second round was at the very beginning of May 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did the communists take part in the elections, or rather, the parties of communist province or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the elections one of the parties that participated was a party that used to be the League of Communists of Croatia. It changed its name and became known as the Party for Democratic Change-League of Communists of Croatia. That was its official name. And it took part in the 1990 elections independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what results did this party achieve, or rather, what the results were of the elections?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: A clear winner of the election with a majority of seats in the parliament, although, in fact, it did not mean that it won the majority of the votes in the elections, it was the Croatian Democratic Union followed by the Croatian Social Liberal Party or Alliance as it was known then and the League of Communists of Croatia, the Party for Democratic Change faired really badly at the elections. It did win some seats in the parliament but with a negligible number of votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I don't want to go into a simultaneous process which was going on in the other republics, but just one question and I don't need you to elaborate. Just tell me if at that time elections were going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina, multi-party elections, that is, in BH?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the Republic of Croatia, the multi-party processes in Bosnia-Herzegovina lagged behind, if you compared them to Croatia. So it was only after the elections were over in Croatia that new parties began to be formed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the elections themselves in Bosnia-Herzegovina were held in November 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, without going into the situation in other republics, although that would be interesting too, but it's sufficient if we look at what happened in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina with respect to this period of time, what was happening - and let's go through the different levels of power - what was happening with the Presidency of the SFRY. Those following in English, I'd just like to tell them that it's page 35 of the English and 39 of the Croatia. Anyway, what happened to the Presidency or what was happening to the Presidency of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The Presidency of the SFRY, which was a parity body and that means that there were the representatives of six republics and two autonomous provinces in it, was in a former blockade, facing a blockade, with a ratio of 4:4; because Serbia, contrary to the constitution, succeeded in having four votes: Serbia and Montenegro and illegally and unlawfully, it took over two votes and seats in all the bodies including the Presidency which belonged to the autonomous provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina, which already in 1989 had been abolished by Serbia. Serbia had abolished their autonomy but they kept their seats in the federal bodies, so that the Presidency, both in 1990 and 1991, was facing a certain blockade. And whenever there was any voting, there was a 4:4 ratio and no decisions could be passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the next force in that structure was the JNA. What happened with the JNA? Did it remain or what should have happened according to the constitution?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: That topic is dealt with in greater detail in the expert report on the basis of the research conducted by different experts, both from Croatia and also from other states on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. And they found that the key changes with respect to transforming the Yugoslav People's Army into a Serb army began to take place in the mid-1980s, that is to say from 1985 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's not go into the details, but as I understand it the changes started earlier on. But what happened at this particular point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: In 1990 on the 17th of August, in actual fact, the JNA openly took the side of the Serb aggression against the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We might go back to that later on in order to explain what this open act of aggression constituted, but I have just one more question in relation to the JNA and that is this: At that time, in the summer of 1990 and 1991, was it quite clear without any dilemmas whatsoever that the JNA -- well, was the JNA what it should have been according to the constitution or not by that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The many steps taken by the JNA in 1990 and 1991 which are set out in detail in the expert report clearly and indubitably showed that it had ceased to be a joint army and that it was a key factor of something that we can call a Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, for those who are following that is to be found on page 48 of the report; in the Croatian version it's page 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This dynamic of change was evolving, as you said, but how would you describe the situation in the Republic of Croatia and Slovenia within the context of their further affiliation to the Yugoslav Federation or the lack of it, their independence at that time, and we're talking about 1990 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Those two states were, on the basis of the first multi-party elections and the referendum that took place later on, undergoing a process of becoming independent and sovereign, and this process is described in greater detail in the expert report. And you have the guide-lines for their work and you can read about that in the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, following on from that, the two republics you mentioned, the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Slovenia, did they, on the basis of an ultimatum, stop all links with the Federation or did they propose some structural changes and organisational changes for a new Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The dissociation of Yugoslavia was a complex process and these two new states, Slovenia and Croatia, were offering a new model, the concept of a new Yugoslav agreement. They offered it up jointly, first of all in September 1990, and they put forward the confederal principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: With respect to this proposal and other similar proposals, were any discussions or meetings held at the level of the representatives of all the republics?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The greatest intensity of meetings of different types within Yugoslavia by different protagonists, especially the protagonists of the new states, was bilateral or trilateral, tripartite, or with six sides taking part and this happened in the first half of 1991. And meetings of this kind were held in their dozens, and the most important of those were six meetings which took place between the leaders, the presidents of the Presidencies of the newly established states and every subsequent meeting was held in the next independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anybody who wants to read about this in greater detail can do so in the report on page 50 of the English, paragraph 3, and on page 58 of the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now you mentioned the referendum in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, earlier I put -- I asked you whether you were a member of a political party, whether you had political activities, and you said no. But I believe that you are going to be a candidate in the presidential election, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the interpretation I got of your question was whether I was a member of any political organisation, and my categoric answer was that I was not. At the beginning of July this year, I put forward my candidatures, an independent candidate, for president of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When is the election planned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those elections will take place, or rather, will start because there will probably be two rounds, either during the first weekend of December this year or the first weekend in January next year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, beyond your academic career you're also an eminent personality in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Over the past 20 years when elementary human rights appeared on the territory of Croatia, I was very active in social life, in the social life of the country, and especially in the civilian life of the country. I was very active in the area of human rights and social cohesion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Therefore my question was not correctly translated which is why there was an ambiguity but now everything is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the referendum in the Croatia. Could you tell us, please, what was the percentage of voters voting for, in favour of, the independent state of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The referendum in Croatia was held on the 19th of May, 1991, and a little over 93 per cent of the voters, those who went out to vote, voted in favour of an independent state of Croatia and 84 per cent went to the -- to vote -- of the population went to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, when Slovenia -- when did Slovenia and Croatia declare their independence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 51 of the English and 59 of the Croatia in the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They proclaimed their independence on the very same day, that is to say their parliaments took the decision for the state to be independent on the 23rd of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said at the beginning that the JNA, in fact, had effected a coup d'etat through its actions. We can go back to that. But just briefly -- well, no, let me ask another question: The Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Slovenia, as you said, proclaimed their independence. Did they implement it or did something else happen?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time it wasn't consumed in formal terms because the European Community exerted pressure both on Slovenia and Croatia; and on the 7th of July, 1991, the so-called Brioni Declaration was passed. And the main decision within that declaration was that the -- that a three-month moratorium be placed on the implementation of these two countries' independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, in your opinion the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Slovenia, by taking that step did they want to demonstrate that they were still ready to continue negotiations and to try and find a solution within some kind of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: In most of their documents and all their prominent bodies did seek a political solution, and as a scholar myself, I would like to say that they couldn't have sought any other solutions since neither of them had any armed force and they were in the process of establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that imply that they had no other way out but to "accept," in quotation marks, the advice given by the European Community?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Neither of them had any other options because already at that time both of them, as indeed the other parts of the former Yugoslavia, were quite clear on the fact that any more serious changes, geopolitical ones, could prevail if it was verified by the international community. That is to say nothing could be done without verification from the European and international community, and this applied to all the parts of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, regarding the Brioni Declaration and the moratorium, you're saying we could only accept the wise advice given by the European Community. Very well. That's one way of looking at things. Now I'd like to know the following, whether the average Croat did feel at the time that this was intervention in sovereign affairs or did the average Croat believe that it was just a friendly declaration or friendly support provided? How was it felt by the man on the -- in the street, you know, the fact that foreign powers were suddenly interfering with the fate of your country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1990 and 1991 in Croatia - and I can testify to this personally because I have a broad circle of contacts and I had them at the time - the predominant view was that the strong security mechanisms in Europe would certainly not allow any armed destruction anywhere in Europe, and that included Yugoslavia. However, as time passed and the Serbian armed aggression gained in force, it -- there was, in the first half of 1991, great dissatisfaction when the European Community made the decisions, even with respect to financial aid to the former Yugoslavia, or rather, the state which barely still existed at the time. And it is in that sense and since Slovenia and Croatia, to be quite specific, had no protection -- that is to say they had no armed forces of their own, it was thought that only the international community could stop the Serbian aggression and there are details about that in the report. And it says that already at that time in the second half of 1991, Alija Izetbegovic and the government of B&H sent out appeals to the European Community to send in monitors and a goodwill mission; however, it fell upon deaf ears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think it's time for the break. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Perhaps for the transcript I've just been told that at the very beginning of the testimony of this witness it was not noted that the expert report of the witness that we are dealing with is in e-court under number 3D003720 [as interpreted] and the CV is 3D03725. This was just for the purposes of the transcript. I'm repeating the first number, 3D03720.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There's one figure too much, Mr. Kovacic, probably one of the first zeros.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D03720.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Only one zero at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you are right. This is what I said. It was wrongly recorded. Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, Professor, you've already said that the JNA aggression was underway. In that situation and we've already mentioned so there's no need for me to repeat this, that this aggression was underway against the newly independent state, there were negotiations going on. Did this new state start functioning as a proper state when we say that it became a state? Did it really function as a state?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. This did not actually take place, or at least not fully, in many different fields. At that moment what was most important was defence. So if we look at defence as the most important thing at that point in time, we can see the extent to which the state did not function. Actually, in 1991 -- or rather, 1991 was the key year for the survival of the new Croatian state and its defence against the armed Serbian aggression. What was of crucial importance that year were volunteers. Croatia did not have armed forces or arms, and in many of the theatres of war, as dictated by the aggressor, there were volunteer -- volunteers who defended the country and then a standard defence, if I can put it that way, came into being. However, volunteers were of crucial importance. It was the Vukovar battle that is a special military phenomenon that was a particular turning point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How and when did a cease-fire come into being, if we can call it that? That is to say when did the aggression against Croatia subside?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: After many cease-fire agreements that were signed unsuccessfully in 1991, finally the international community organised the following: On the 2nd of January, 1992, the so-called Sarajevo cease-fire was signed and it meant a kind of cessation in the Serbian attempts to take other parts of Croatia. The aggression was then diverted to the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. About a quarter of Croatian territory remained occupied, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you please just explain what you mean when you say that the aggression was then diverted to the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Let me ask you specifically. What happened with the JNA forces in Croatia when the cease-fire came into effect and when UN protected areas were created, where did the JNA forces go?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1991, again as organised by the international community, negotiations took place in Croatia, certain agreements were reached, and there was a process of withdrawing a significant part of the forces of the JNA from many areas in the Republic of Croatia. They withdrew from the occupied zones too after the cease-fire, and most of these forces came to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was full of armaments anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this period you pointed out the importance of the report of the so-called Badinter Commission. Could you please explain to me, as briefly as possible, why that document is something that you consider to be so important, rather, this position taken by the Badinter Commission. You write about it on page 53 in the English version, page 62 in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you answer that question, I have a follow-up question to put to you that relates to your previous answer. It took a while for me to phrase it properly, given how important it is. You said that the international community achieved the withdrawal of the JNA from the Republic of Croatia, a free territory -- the free territory and the occupied territory. They then moved into the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When I was listening to you, I wondered why the international community did not require at the time that they withdraw via areas which would have enabled them to go straight back to Serbia without occupying Bosnia-Herzegovina in any way. Was this something which had been contemplated or not, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question would merit a complex answer; however, the Serbian aggressor treated the territory of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina as a single theatre of war. I refer to that extensively in my expert report and I don't want to go into the reasons now as to why the decision was made to continue the total aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina and to conserve, as it were, the situation in the Republic of Croatia. One of the reasons is that it became clear to the Serb aggressor and to the international community that Serbia no longer had armed forces that could break Croatia fast, especially not after the battle of Vukovar, where the Serbian aggressor suffered significant losses. There was a fear that the continuation of a war between Serbia and Croatia would spill over into central Europe and further on. So from a political and military point of view, the aggression was fully transferred to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and therefore, the forces of the former JNA which had become the key part of the Serbian army. In accordance with this agreement, the JNA was no longer called the JNA. They became new military formations in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, but most of these forces were transferred to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question lies at the heart of a theory you put forward in your expert report. You are saying that the Serbs were faced with a single warring party, which were the Croats and the Muslims. This is what you state in your report. And now you are saying that when they withdraw -- withdrew in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they withdrew into what they considered to be the territory of the other warring faction they were faced with. Does this mean that in the eyes of the international community, there was a clear understanding of the situation, but the fact was that the problem lay in Croatia and not in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that this was done knowingly? This is just an assumption I'm making.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From a phenomenological point of view, there is no doubt that the problem was transferred to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course the reasons and the interests involved had to do with all the protagonists in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, including the international community. Everyone had their own motives. That could be explored further and discussed further. However, there is no doubt that the focus of the aggression was shifted to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and we can say that the situation in Croatia was conserved, as it were. Whenever I speak about the Serbian aggression, I never say the "Serb aggression," because that would mean that it was an ethnic thing denoting the Serbs. I always say "Serbian" because it means that it's the Serbian state that organised this, and there were different protagonists involved. Ethnically you can look at Croats too, there were some Croats who engaged in this aggression in the Serbian army. On the other hand, there were ethnic Serbs among those who defended the Republic of Croatia. Therefore, I believe it would be a good thing to define things very precisely, so not ethnically, terminologically, but from this other point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we just briefly go back to the question about the significance of the Badinter Commission for this entire process. Why was it that important for us?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: It was only in the beginning of September that the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia started to function. One of its most important parts was the arbitration commission, the so-called Badinter Commission, which gave this international commission opinions, or rather, answers to different questions that had to do with legal and historic questions. There were several such questions involved. All of them were important, but I think that you mean what happened in December. I haven't actually referred to this page of the expert opinion. I think that you are referring to the position, stating that the dissolution of Yugoslavia has reached its final stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is correct, indeed. At that point in time, Yugoslavia was in the final stages of its dissolution and I supported that with some additional conclusions in this expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For those who are following this in English, the page is 51 and 52 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So in order to complete this particular period of time, after that what happened was the international recognition of the Republic of Croatia and since we've already made this comparison, also Slovenia was internationally recognised; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The process of preparing the international recognition of these two states took place at an international level, at the level of all of Europe, and it culminated on the 15th of January, 1992, by the international recognition of Croatia and Slovenia by the European Community, the EC. As for Bosnia and Herzegovina, a precondition was set, namely that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be recognised as a state only after a referendum took place involving the participation of all the citizens of the country and on the basis of internationally accepted standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that we have now come to a topic that you discussed in the second part of your report entitled: "Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1990 to 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Croatian it is page 63. In English it is page 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: First of all, now that we have come to that part, perhaps you could explain to the Judges, it is a very basic fact, as far as you're concerned, but we want the Court to familiarise itself with what matters to us. As opposed to the other republics of the SFRY, how was the question of peoples resolved in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I'm talking about the period while the SFRY still existed.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina was the only republic of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The only republic of the former Yugoslavia, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that from the 1970s onwards, and this was finally defined by the 1974 constitution -- well, this was a very specific characteristic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and very often that is why Bosnia-Herzegovina was called a small-scale Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think that all know the answer to this question, but these were what peoples?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to speak of them in terms of the 1991 census. It was the Muslim Bosniaks, and I explain in my expert report why I call them that; and Serbs; and Croats, the three constituent peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned that a referendum took place. What were the results -- or rather, when did it finally take place, this referendum?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The referendum was held during two days, the last days of the month of February -- rather, the 29th of February and the 1st of March, 1992. That's when it was held. Somewhat over 64 per cent of the inhabitants of Bosnia-Herzegovina voted in this referendum in favour of state independence; out of that number, 99.4 per cent voted. However, the referendum was held in spite of the protests of the Serbs throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say out of 109 municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina the referendum was held in 107 municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For those who are following this in English, it is pages 86 and 87 of the expert report, that is where this is contained, what the professor referred to just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, if we look at the official figures as to how many inhabitants of Bosnia-Herzegovina voted and how many of them belonged to which one of the three peoples, how could the referendum be declared successful if how many people voted in favour of a particular proposition?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Not a single one of the constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina had a proper majority on its own. In order to have any kind of decision reached, at least two of the constituent peoples had to participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: According to the existing information we have, what were the two peoples that voted?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Muslim Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So apart from the Muslims, the Croats were the ones who contributed to the success of the referendum; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, without the participation of the Croats, the referendum would have failed -- or rather, no decision could have been made about the independence of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And, Professor, this was so despite the fact that there was a great deal of disagreement among the Croats about the actual wording of the referendum question. Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As the referendum was being prepared, the Muslim Bosniaks and Croats alike did not at any point in time bring into question the final result, which was the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was some disagreement about the wording of the question, where the Croats tried to include in the question the rights that they enjoyed at that time and at that level. In other words, the status of a constituent people. It was not adopted, but the Croats participated in the referendum because that was the prerequisite of the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state. And in fact, the Croats voted for the -- at the referendum for the question that was worded by the Muslim ruling structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, now we come to the question whether the Croatian leadership -- the Croatian institutions in any way participated in the law being among the Croatian population in Bosnia and Herzegovina in favour of them participating in the referendum.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the time when the referendum was being prepared, and in particular while it was being conducted, the key institutions of the Republic of Croatia lobbied in a number of ways, advocated and promoted the participation of Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina in the referendum and their vote for the independence of the state of the -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, please, did the Republic of Croatia or its political leadership have any vested interest in Bosnia and Herzegovina becoming an independent state?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. The interest of the Republic of Croatia in that was manifold. It was in the interest of the Republic of Croatia in having Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent and integral state. I don't want to now go into reasons which are elaborated in my expert report. It's enough to just look at the map and to realise that Bosnia and Herzegovina or Croatia cannot in any sense, including the sense of security, stable states if there are no stability in the other states. So one state cannot be stable without the other being stable. There were some additional reasons too which were present as Croatian priorities because one-fourth of the Croatian territory was occupied at the time and most of those areas bordered with Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the possibility of re-integration of that territory into republic -- into the Republic of Croatia depended to a great extent on the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after the referendum the results were declared, and did Bosnia then gain international recognition as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As the international community had stipulated, the referendum was conducted under its auspices, and then on the 7th of April the process of international recognition of a new independent state, the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, began.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that you we have the fundamental elements of the situation at the time. Just one more question perhaps. So when Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 7th of April, 1992, gained international recognition - and I would like to remind you that I've asked the same question about Croatia - did it function as a state should or at least as we believe a state should function? So was it able to exercise all the prerogatives of its power?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: As has been explained in some detail in the expert report, Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time found itself in very difficult situation, both from the point of view of security, the effort to organise the state, and the -- its capability to function. The situation it faced was much more difficult than Croatia did in 1990 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At page 78 and -- 78 in the English version, 93 in the Croatian version you talk about the emergence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Could you please explain to us -- well, it's explained in detail. But could you please tell us in just a couple of sentences what the purpose was, what the objectives were, and why, indeed, it was established -- or rather, let me cut to the chase. I think we've talked about that here in court for a long time. But could you please turn to page 95 through 99. That's 79 through 82 in the English version. We have the photocopies of various forms that you put on those pages. What argument do you support with these forms by way of an example?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, since there are various stereotypes present in the public about what the Croatian community and later the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna actually was, in addition to other facts that I mention in my expert report, here I provided on a number of pages copies -- well, these are official documents that were published in the Official Gazette, copies of various civilian, military, and educational and other documents showing that without any exceptions and systematically the state, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, gets top billing, followed by one of its territorial elements, the Croatian Community, later Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
