utterances.text: Thank you very much. When it comes to setting up some infrastructure on the borders facing the Republic of Croatia, what kind of designations were present there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is yet another very obvious and mass fact which speaks about the nature and character of the Croatian Community -- Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Decisions were made, formal decisions, vis-a-vis the Republic of Croatia and also border crossings were set up between the two states; whereas in the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina there were no such decisions or designations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I conclude on the basis of your response that the HZ HB did -- that had it not set up those border crossings and signs, they would not have existed; is this your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of the arguments or premises coming from that. The central government, as I explained in detail in my expert report, supporting with documentary evidence, was blocked. It was unable to function in a number of fundamental areas including the setting up of borders. So it is true that had the local authorities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna set up those border crossings, they would not have existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to go through all this very briefly. But tell me, what act marks the beginning of the aggression of the JNA and the Bosnian Serbs against Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, there's something that's still on the screen, and I believe it's quite important. Counsel just asked you to explain why there is the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina followed by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. You are saying that this is a regional entity. Very well. I'm sure that you know that some might believe that it is a state within a state. So could you please tell us why you can affirm that it is a regional entity. Could you expand on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, according to a number of decrees, decisions, and other documents that were issued in the Croatian Community or Republic of Herceg-Bosna, including the decision on the foundation thereof, it is defined that it is a political, cultural, economical, and regional whole that respects the -- or recognises the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When we speak about the state politicological, in term of political science, sociologically, and I also think in legal terms it is quite clear what it means, a state. It means that there has to be sovereignty. It means that no higher power is recognised in terms of sovereignty. But when we're talking about a region or a regional whole, I would not say -- I would not use the term "entity," because the term "entity" gained other connotations as the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina continued. We could see, on the basis of the decisions on the border crossings and some other decisions, that it was a regional whole that was created in order to defend itself, and in some decisions with the interim nature is stressed -- in other words, that it would continue to operate only during the threat of war or with the state of war. Those who say that it was a state, I would like to say that I think that those arguments are unfounded and not objective from a scientific point of view, but a layperson is always entitled to present their views in a pluralist society. But it is difficult on the basis of the documents that I've looked at and all my work on my expert reports, it is difficult for any scholar complying with scholarly standards would be able to say that the Croatian Community or later Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was something that we could label a state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please look at page 82 in the English version. There is a document in your own language. Could we please have page 82 in English on the screen. We don't need to have it in B/C/S because I'm interested about the document itself and it is in B/C/S and the English version. This is the document, and I note Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in small print, and below in large print, there's reference to Herceg-Bosna. So how can you explain this? Shouldn't it have been the opposite in terms of the size of the print?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why that is so, well there are several interpretations. But at any rate, the size of the font is one of the elements that can be used when one analyses those documents. According to another analysis, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is at the top in those documents and in other documents too. There are some documents that I've provided here where it is different. Now, who the graphic designer was, I don't know. But the most important thing is when you look at those documents in the other context, the decisions and everything that existed in the actual fact, as we've spoken about here and in my -- I spoke about that in my expert report, it is undoubted that on the basis of the size of the font as a graphic element it is difficult to conclude, in the face of all the other documents, to conclude selectively that it was a state. It is my opinion, scientific opinion and any other kind of opinion, if it had been a state, there would not have been the -- the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina would not have been mentioned at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I read your report from beginning to end. I read it over and over again. And at one point in time, I noted that you said that in history the population of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were -- they were all illiterate, almost all of them were illiterate. I was looking at this, and I was wondering the following: What about, you know, the farmer, the dieppe [phoen], okay. He's illiterate but he had good eyesight, you know, and he sees the design and what is the conclusion that he draws from the design, from these fonts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Statistical data about the illiteracy in Bosnia and Herzegovina are presented for the period of Austro-Hungary. I used the data presented in another study by another scholar. I think the population is 97 per cent; 97 per cent of the population was illiterate at the time. In the 1990s, when those documents that we're talking about were made, the majority of the population was literate, able to read. But if I were to answer your question from the point of view of logic, if the person is illiterate, the size of the font means nothing to them because they cannot read them anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. A person cannot read. But Herceg-Bosna is something that he must comprehend? No? Let me sum up. You're saying that we shouldn't place any importance on this kind of document because this kind of document must be put back within an entire set -- a larger set of documents. Is that what you're telling us? If I'm wrong, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Professor, I would like to have a follow-up question to what the President asked you about. First of all, I believe that when you answered a few minutes ago that herein on page, I believe, 50, second line that it is written that the -- and I quote: "I think the population is 97 per cent; 97 per cent of the population," you repeated, "was illiterate at the time, in the 1990s." I believe that it is a mistake and probably you may have spoken about the 1890s because you said in a previous sentence that statistical data about the literacy in Bosnia and Herzegovina are presented for the period of Austro-Hungary, which would mean that you spoke about -- the situation from 1868, that is, 1870, 1880, 1890, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: -- although I have certain doubts, myself, that the illiteracy was so high that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I am reminded that I speak too fast. Okay. Then let me repeat that although I'm afraid probably that figure of 97 per cent is too high as far as the illiteracy is concerned towards the end of the 19th century, but, of course, it is a question of facts and it could be found out. But I believe that the very fact that that was already -- that that was already towns, the Croat towns itself, and Sarajevo, et cetera, I fear that it is somehow overstated and exaggerated, but, of course, again I say I stand to be corrected, and it could be looked into it -- and, frankly, I also know that this very issue is not so important for us now if we are dealing with your report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The punctuation was not recorded correctly. There should have been a full stop. The full stop was at the wrong place. The sentence began with the words "in the 1990s."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, the interpreters, for clarifying that it was a mistake most probably in the transcript and later on also there is a chance to make the relevant corrections over there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise if I made a mistake, if I said something else. The data pertains to the late 19th century, so you are right, it's the Austro-Hungarian period. I did not do any research into that. I simply took over this information from a study done by a scholar who did research into that period and that area. I would not now go into estimates, or rather, what this data was based on and what methodology was used. And after all, it is not really relevant for our purposes here. But at any rate, that pertains to the end of the 19th century, so more than 100 years ago. That's not the information that I obtained. It's contained in a footnote. The reference is in the footnote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you did not answer my question when my fellow Judge put his question a bit fast before you could answer mine. So I put it again. I wonder when you read the document such as the one we have here with the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with very small print and with the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna with big font should be considered in an even bigger perspective.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No -- well, as a scholar, I don't consider any document to be unimportant. It can be very important, secondary, tertiary, or whatever. But if we look at some other documents that I have photocopied here, we can see that there are other examples, examples of a different kind. For example, in the Croatian text, number 97 -- well, you can see that where it says the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the title, you see that written in bigger letters on some forms. On the other forms, the letters are the same size. And on other forms again you have them written in different ways. So one of the conclusions is that it was not systematised. There wasn't a systematic way of writing this. But if there were any further consequences from the document, then most probably on all the documents, the font size would be like that. But on all the documents that I saw, including the written documents, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was always first. And on different documents the font size would change. Now, whether there were any intentions in these specific documents, whether they wanted to achieve anything through these documents, I don't know. And it can't be a general conclusion because there are documents, as I say, where the letters Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is in a bigger font size, but in others it's smaller but always in the same place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you're right, there are a number of documents that go against the fact that in some other documents Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is in small font and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is in large font. I agree with that, but look at page 81, documents on the registration of vehicles. Could we please have page 81 on the screen, Mr. Registrar. Thank you. Let's assume that a driver is touring and ends up in Finland, driving in Finland. You know where Finland is, I'm sure. And the policeman from Finland and asking him for his registration card. Don't you think that the Finnish policeman is going to be a bit confused when he is going to see this kind of document? This is an assumption, you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At all events you are right when it comes to the inconsistencies of the system of these documents, and anybody who sees that might think -- well, whatever they like. They can think whatever they like. That's their right. But the fact remains and one fact that springs to view, and I mentioned this when talking about the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, I emphasised as far as that community is concerned and as far as the overall structure of Croats in BH are concerned that they were in a very poor organisational state. They were heterogenous, both structurally and on an individual level. They were unbalanced. They were reactive, and so on and so forth. Now, in view of the fact of when these documents came into being, I think had anybody arrived with respect to the catastrophic security situation and the generally bad situation in the area, they wouldn't even notice these documents or any other ones for that matter, or any other ones for that matter, that were notes in better situations. Because all that's important here is life itself, to save one's life, and cultural issues and all other issues were marginalised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just another question as a follow-up. It might be interesting with respect to the question that the Presiding Judge asked about the Finnish police and how they would react. Now, Professor, in all the documents about the HZ HB and all the negotiation documents, documents that were issued, decisions that were passed, and so on and so forth, that there was confirmation that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had pretensions of being an internationally recognised subject.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: I saw a large number of documents, only part of which were included in this expert report, but I did not come across a single document anywhere which would be an explicit example of this or which would contain any such thing in an implicit way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, those pretensions, could you read between the lines perhaps, looking at the basic documents on the constitution of the community of Herceg-Bosna, would that be read between the lines somewhere?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: I claim that it would not because I looked through the Narodni List and the collection they have, and always in first place whenever there's any document or decision you have the state, that is to say the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that comes first; and in a whole series of various other documents, without a doubt the position taken was that the original state of the Croats was Bosnia-Herzegovina, the mother state, and that was not brought into question anywhere in any official document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now to go back to where we were, and I'd just like to ask you to give me brief answers. When and by what act did the JNA aggression and the Serbs start against Bosnia-Herzegovina? What was the defining moment?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The start of an armed aggression can be dated to 1991. Examples are quoted in the expert report itself, from May onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it true and correct that the JNA armed members of the SDS and other Serbs living in Bosnia-Herzegovina even before these actions undertaken in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and we have testimony to that in various documents and reports and writings and testimony from the then-actors who were positioned in the central powers in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From your answers so far and from the expert report itself, it would follow - and this is a subject we discussed here on many occasions - that at the point in time when the aggression was launched the start of armed forces, the establishment of armed forces began in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you tell me something then about the Patriotic League. What was the Patriotic League and who set it up?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The Patriotic League was a military and political organisation which came into being within the Muslim Bosniak structures in Bosnia and Herzegovina and within -- most within the SDA, or rather, the party of Muslims, Bosniaks in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the actors themselves, that is to say the people who participated in that can testify to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What about the Territorial Defence, did that exist at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: It was one of the first armed forces which burgeoned and in 1992 they -- these forces became renamed and called the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, bearing in mind the strength of the Territorial Defence and its importance and on the basis of the concept of total national defence in Yugoslavia, wasn't that a very strong force when the aggression started?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in realistical terms it should have been a strong force to reckon with in the numerical terms. However, since the aggressor, or rather, the JNA, already in 1990 took weapons away from the Territorial Defence, both in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Croatia as well as in the other republics, well, for the most part at least, then the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was confronted with a series of problems which are discussed and described in my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, on those grounds can we say that the Territorial Defence started out as a very weak power, it had -- it didn't have enough weapons or equipment?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Part of the Territorial Defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not cross over to the Serbian side, so that side was very poorly armed and poorly equipped. They didn't have enough uniforms and so on. And just to illustrate that, let me say that the leaders from the BH army testified that during the first [indiscernible] of the war and according to them that was 1992 to 1993, most of the soldiers belonging to the Territorial Defence, that is to say the BH army, spent in civilian clothes and footwear. And even in 1994 when the number of soldiers was at its peak, they still did not have one rifle per soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what about the HOS, who was that, the H-O-S, what kind of military force was that and to whom did it belong?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The HOS was a volunteer armed force which appeared on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina predominantly in areas where the Croats were the majority population. However, HOS was composed of both Croats and Muslims, Bosniaks, and it was an army or a group of people which was established and supervised by the Croatian party of rights from Croatia. So the headquarters for HOS was formed already in January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us just briefly the relationship between the HOS and the HVO at the very beginning while the members were all volunteers and later on when they were better organised, say in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The relationship between the two differed. That would be my best answer, my best shot, and it depended on the local circumstances, the situation that prevailed and temporal considerations. But ultimately a conflict broke out between the two, and from 1992 onwards, HOS gradually -- or rather, from mid-1992, HOS gradually ceased to exist, either as a group or individuals, and it disseminated to become the HVO or BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just one more question with respect to HOS. What was their political platform? What did they want to achieve? What kind of Bosnia were they fighting for?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The basic political platform of HOS was a platform of the Croatian party of rights, which at that time was unequivocal in advocating a Croatia up to the Drina River, that is to say Croatia including the territory of the state of Croatia and the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can I know how much time I have left. Could the Registrar tell me how much time I had left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A while ago you had 20 minutes left, that is at least five minutes ago. I believe you must have something like 10 or 15 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I thought as much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor -- you have nine minutes left, to be precise. Mr. Kovacic, you have nine minutes left. Professor, Mr. Kovacic asked you a question about the HOS and you told us that this was an offshoot of a political party, the party of rights. We have heard a lot of testimony about that. General Praljak has also testified, and as things stand today, the question I have relates to this. At the time in 1992/1993, what was Tudjman doing in the political arena? Was he working on the basis of a consensus or did he have to cooperate with various trends in the Croatian political life? The HOS could have been one of these trends but was reduced to nothing. You lived through this period, and as far as you remember, did President Tudjman represent the aspiration of all the people who had voted for him or did he represent the sum total of various different trends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the time has come for me to ask you to separate your one question into smaller questions, because I think you have four or five different questions within that one. So could you ask them again, please, one by one. That will prevent me from going into the subject at length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I would like to know is the following: At the time when President Tudjman had been elected, had he been elected on the basis of a political platform which all the voters identified with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first presidential elections under the new constitution for the president of the Republic of Croatia happened at the beginning of August 1992. And at those elections the over -- well, Franjo Tudjman was elected president by an overwhelming majority. Since it was the electoral right of each and every voter to vote as they saw fit, we can say that Tudjman was elected by the will of the majority of voters in the Republic of Croatia. Now, what the structure was in the social or political sense is difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have heard a lot of witnesses here. General Praljak told us himself that several Croats living in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina were entitled to vote in Croatia because they had dual nationality. Therefore, when an election took place, presidential election, or an election in the Sabor, a Croatian living in Bosnia and Herzegovina was entitled to vote. What I would like to know is this: When President Tudjman was elected by Croats living in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for instance, the question I'm putting to you is when he prepared his political platform did he need to factor these people in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be a reasonable assumption, both for Tudjman and for other politicians. But the following should also be taken into account. At that time and today it was not only Croats who lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina who had Croatian citizenship, but also a significant number of Bosniak Muslims did and a number of Serbs as well. Now, this would be the logic of political thinking. In accordance with the number of votes they have, politicians would certainly take that into account. However, viewed on the whole, those who have the right to vote in the Republic of Croatia and who are also citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they are not a significant factor in terms of prevalent vote, either in parliamentary elections or presidential elections in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying that those who lived in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina voted in the Sabor or in the parliament or voted when there was a presidential election, but these did not represent a significant number of people for this to matter. Now, as far as a question of Herceg-Bosna is concerned, as far as President Tudjman is concerned, was this a minor issue or was this a crucial issue? I'm talking now in political terms. I'm not talking in strategic terms. One moment. General Praljak, please sit down because this might affect the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here comes the answer. My opinion is partly contained in the expert report, so it is well-founded and it is in the introductory part of the third part of the expert report, speaking of the relationship between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the introduction, I very succinctly, but very objectively and correctly, stated what the strategic interests of the Republic of Croatia were, that is to say of the institution of the Presidency, or rather, the president, who was Franjo Tudjman, in relation to the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina and developments therein. Up until 1995, particularly after 1992 when Croatia received international recognition, the reintegration of the occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia became a priority. And on the basis of my entire expert report, especially the third part where in a very concrete and well-documented manner on the basis of a large number of documents of a political and military nature from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I'm primarily referring to the documents of the Army of the BiH and the main institutions of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is a political interest involved and a security and military interest involved on the part of Franjo Tudjman. And it was aimed at the entire state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Otherwise it would be difficult to explain the large continued support that I explained in detail in the third part, that the Republic of Croatia institutionally provided to the military and political segment of the central authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So if I were to make a hierarchy, so to speak, of primary interest were developments throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. In view of the strategic interests of the Republic of Croatia in that period, the area that was covered by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and also by Croats who were in minority -- well, those were of secondary importance. Synthetically this can be seen from what Franjo Tudjman signed in Washington and Dayton. The political outcome of that was, as is the case today, the constitutional position of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina that was there at the time when they left Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me break down my initial question. I had questions because the strategic aspect had been left out. I was about to discuss this. We have heard witnesses and General Praljak has told us that in light of the fact that there was an aggression, President Tudjman had to take this into account, which means according to General Praljak and other people that an effort was made to supply in arms the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the ABiH, because if this had not been done, the Serbs would have broken through the front line and would have constituted a threat. Therefore, President Tudjman needed to take an interest in what was happening in Herceg-Bosna. Do you agree with the people that claim this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In part. Actually, most of the occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia - and that was the priority of their integration from the point of view of the interests of the Republic of Croatia - they bordered with the areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina where Croats were not a majority. The second fact to be taken into account is that in terms of logistic and other survival Croats received their support through the other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia had to be taken into account. That is to say those parts had more importance because of all these factors. If we had a map here, I could show you exactly what I mean. Herceg-Bosna -- or rather, this area that we should look at, it had a certain degree of significance but not -- it was not a primary priority. The area of Herceg-Bosna was important for the southern parts of the Republic of Croatia, that is to say they're very narrow. So from a security point of view, they were easy to destabilise. As for these southern parts the area -- the area of what we call Herzegovina was important or what we could call, in this sense, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. But viewed on the whole, and that is obvious if one looks at the map with all this information that I referred to, that objectively speaking for the Republic of Croatia other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina were far more important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I put my question and meaning to address a political aspect. That is when General Praljak was like a Jack-in-a-box and he jumped up. I don't know if he wants to say something. Whatever the case may be he cannot testify. What is it you wanted to say? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I'm not going to testify, Your Honour, I've had enough. But the question that you put, please, could it have the right time sequence, 1991, the elections in 1991, and then further on. You are speaking of a fact as if it did not have a dynamic characteristic. It is always important for your question to have this dynamic characteristic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I admit that dates have to be referenced with a great deal of precision. The Prosecution steps in sometimes to correct the dates. As far as my question is concerned, I had not established a distinction when I took into account the time factor. My question applied, as far as you are concerned, to 1992 and 1993, or in light of the time factor, do you think you would change your answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is my understanding of your question. It is comprehensive and that is how I answered it. Of course we can go into individual time-periods, but then we would have to look at matters at a different level too, what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina in addition to this, what happened in Croatia, what the attitude of the international community was; but that is for you to decide and for you to say. I think, Your Honour, that as we've gone into all these details - that is my feeling at least, if it's wrong, you please tell me - we started this series of questions -- I don't want you to think that I'm evading anything or avoiding something or trying to dodge some of your questions, I think that you put the questions of the HOS and you asked about the state institution of the Republic of Croatia and Franjo Tudjman, their attitude towards the HOS and its armed force, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before the break we addressed this, but I shall stream-line my question and address a part of the question. We all know that President Tudjman was campaigning in a presidential election. As far as you remember, in the Croatian political life were there a change or were the voters still in the same state of mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first elections took place in 1990. The second ones in 1992. And the situation in Croatia was equally difficult. In a way, I think that the prevalent feeling was the same, including the elections of 1995. That was reflected in the presidential elections, the parliamentary elections, and local election as well. The voters gave their confidence to President Tudjman and the party that he headed, the HDZ. However, at that time -- well, we're moving to a different level, aren't we? At that time in Croatia, there were intensive political conflicts going on of different interests that could be noted in the case of the HDZ itself. The first major stratification of the HDZ, or rather, the rift in the HDZ in 1994 and this led to a parliamentary crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question is an extremely delicate question. I need to be extremely careful. This is in the form of an assumption. The basic voter in 1991 and 1994 before the rift inside the HDZ which you have just talked about, let's take the case of a standard voter. As far as you know, because you're a specialist in these matters, i.e., the history of your country, as far as the Croats in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina are concerned, what do you think the standard voter wanted? Do you think he or she wanted two republics, perhaps even being part of a federation or a confederation? Or did such voter want a unique, single, republic in which Croatia would have taken in the geographical area of Herceg-Bosna? What do you think the man in the street, the voter, thought about these various options? If you are able to answer of course, otherwise let us know if you can't, which I fully understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, their first or top priority was security for sure. The Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina are a constituent people, and they achieved that through their long life in that territory. According to the research carried out by my institute and the research carried out sociologists who study mentality and other things, these people really feel that Bosnia-Herzegovina is their home. From a political point of view, from 1990 when Bosnia-Herzegovina started disintegrating as a state, since the Croats are the weakest in Bosnia-Herzegovina if we are going to be very explicit, they were the smallest people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so in view of the entire history dynamics involved in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this instability, there is no doubt about that, this instability and lack of security, so due to many historic experiences, even those that were within living memory dating back to the Second World War, for example. So when this new card game was being played in the area, if I can use that figure of speech, they saw somewhat of a guarantee in the fact that they could have an entity of their own in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that was explicitly stated with regard to several peace plans that were offered by the international community. That was a specific indicator too. The Croats were the only ones who accepted all the peace plans offered by the international community. As a rule, they signed them without any strings attached and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not answering my question. You're putting yourself in the shoes of a Croat who lives in Bosnia-Herzegovina. My question had to do with a Croatian voter who lives in Zagreb, for instance, what was his or her point of view as regarded the Croats in Herceg-Bosna? This is what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is difficult to speak about that because there are no reliable studies, but let me share with you an impression but this is not strong scientific argument. Some interests, political and other interest, in the power struggle in the Republic of Croatia, in social and public life in all of its aspects, continuously labelled the Croats from Herzegovina as negative, universally negative. So that the term Herzegovinian, unfortunately, is used to discriminate against those people, generally, and it has become to have a negative connotation and discriminatory connotation. This stereotype had been created in the Croatian public through concerted efforts of the media and one could analyse it. This is my impression. But if you were to look at the media in Croatia and if you were to analyse it using methods that exist, what the positions were -- what the views were expressed in the public life about Herzegovinians, negative rather than neutral views would prevail. Now, I don't know whether I've responded to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. It's time to have a break now. After the break, Mr. Kovacic, you will have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Witness, I had something to tell you. I told you earlier but I will repeat it. We will end the session at 7.00 p.m. and sometimes we're quite rushed and I don't want to miss having -- I want to tell you what I have to say. We know that you are an eminent Croat personality, so please do not contact the media to tell them anything about the hearing. Please don't tell them anything, otherwise, you know, the Prosecutor might say that you contacted the media, that you were under oath, and that you violated this oath and so forth and so on. So once you're back in your country, you can say what you want, but up until then you're under oath. So I must tell you not to contact the media. Okay. Please answer so it's on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I have understood you fully and I will comply with your instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: Mr. President, I have just have one, I think, very important remark regarding the transcript. Maybe it was translated on French but it was not translated on English, this is page 66 or 67. I don't have LiveNote, so I am not able to follow that, but I am sure and I checked with my colleagues as well that two times, at least one time very clearly, witness answered on your question, I'm now paraphrasing: Main goal of Croats was to ensure the same level of rights as they achieved in 1990. It was the very crux of the answer and it was not translated. This is not just technical, minor mistake; I think this is important to be said. Maybe you heard that on French, but on English there is no such wording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Professor, can you confirm what was said which was that you made an explicit reference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. This is correct. Several times in the context of your questions, this is precisely what I answered, that this was the fundamental motive, reason, or interest driving the Croats in BH, and I explained why I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So just to go back a little bit, we started listing all the groups that were active in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We stopped at the HOS and could you please tell me -- well, I don't think there's no need for me to ask again what the HVO was. We have been hearing about that for three years, but could you please tell us very briefly, really very briefly, what are the basic characteristics of the HVO as a defence force?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: The basic features or characteristics are listed in some detail in the expert report and there are documents from that time that made the same assessment. It was an army that was manned by volunteers and it had serious of defects throughout the time of its existence. If you compare it with the regular armies, the personnel were not trained and it was very closely linked with the local unit, with the local administrative units. It was a big problem. The central funding was not implemented. They were funded locally -- well, I could go into that, but it is all explained in great detail in the expert report, so I do not want to waste your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. This element, the voluntary basis for its organisation, why do you describe these people as volunteers? What are the different elements? We have different situations here. Could you please clarify that a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, they came into being as volunteers. They were untrained, and throughout the war, it was impossible to train them. There were no military institutions or personnel who could carry out this training. So the problem -- one of the key problems of the HVO in general was how to set up something that would be an army of the kind that we are -- used to see in regular, well-organised states.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: After the general mobilisation was called up in the area affecting all the conscripts and call-up papers were even sent to some individuals, and if we have a soldier, ex-conscript, ex-, who received the call-up papers, did they have to comply with them and go and report to their unit?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: No. There were no mechanisms in place to implement the mobilisation, the call-up, using some coercion and there was no prevalent opinion among the people that something had to be done in terms of the draft and in terms of those who volunteered to join so that the hierarchy, the chain of command, was simply non-existent or at a very, very low level. You can see that from a number of documents and examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to move on to some minor questions because I don't have much time. They pertain to the chapter: "The relationship between the Republic of Croatia and Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." That's at page 128 in the English version. I would like to ask you two or three things if I may. You can surely give me a yes or no answer. Did the Republic of Croatia recognise the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, together with the USA and the European Union, it was the first to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. So it was immediately after Bosnia and Herzegovina declared its independence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, was an agreement on friendship signed by the two states?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, friendship and co-operation, as I state in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And even after this agreement was signed, were there efforts to establish full co-operation, especially since October 1992 until April 1992, so in that time-period, or rather, April 1993 -- so were there efforts made by the Croatian side to establish full co-operation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I elaborate that in my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: After the recognition of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the Republic of Croatia, were diplomatic relations established?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in line with that, did the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina open its embassy in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in addition to the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb, did the Croatian government also approve the opening or setting up of a logistics centre for the BH army that was active in the embassy?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the embassy and there were many other logistics centres, either of the BH army as a whole or some units or groups that had an interest in supporting the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did Croatia ever, to the best of your knowledge, or is there any evidence to that effect, I mean scholarly evidence, did it disrupt the work of those centres in any way and their functioning?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: No, and information from various state bodies from Bosnia and Herzegovina, its army, and people working in those logistics centres speak about that very persuasively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were wounded soldiers of the BH army treated medically in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and there is comprehensive documentation about that in the Republic of Croatia, and I provide synthetic information about that with the sources in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The medical treatment of the BH army soldiers, did it continue even after a large-scale conflict between the HVO and the BH army erupted, so from the summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: And as to the quality of the treatment provided, we can see that from various letters of gratitude sent by various units and individuals by the BH army to the Croatian medical institutions and physicians, doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor -- well, we have seen this here before but let us make this quite clear. Did a single tonne of food and medicines, could it enter Bosnia and Herzegovina using any other root apart from going through the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, any assistance that reached Bosnia and Herzegovina could only reach it through the territory of the Republic of Croatia because the other borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina faced the Serbian aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did various humanitarian organisations operate in the Republic of Croatia without any disruptions and their sole purpose was to provide aid to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to an unusually high degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were there organisations among them that dealt with providing aid only to the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Most of those organisations in the Republic of Croatia did precisely that. You have specific information and data in my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did aid reach Bosnia and Herzegovina from overseas?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from all the continents apart from South America.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And was this humanitarian aid then transferred from ships to shore in Croatian ports?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in huge quantities, in particular in the port of Ploca. I think more than 611.000 tonnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And there are data to that effect from various sources about everything that I've asked you about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is very concrete, specific, accurate documentation about that from various sources, international, Croatian, and BH sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, for your answers to the questions posed by the Praljak Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that we have just gone briefly through the expert report. We can see just how detailed it is and how much information is provided. All we wanted to do was demonstrate its weight and value, and since we don't have much time for the rest of our Defence case, we consider that that suffices and this gives the other Defence teams a chance to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Professor, I have a follow-up question regarding the work done by you. You said that the international community played a crucial role in solving the conflict. In your report, you mention what the international community did, talking about the Lisbon Declaration. Then you talk about the Vance-Owen Plan, then the Stoltenberg plan, and you end up with the negotiations under the aegis of the USA which will result in the Dayton agreements of March 1st, 1994. Obviously you have taken a close look at all this and there is a question that springs to my mind. Why it that Europe with all these succession of plans failed in the end and how come -- why is it that the US managed to find a solution in March suddenly? Can you explain this if you have an idea of course or maybe you can say that it's too complex, and I'll just withdraw my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question I would say is a key question. Now, if we speak about motives the answer can be complex, but in essence it's very simple. The international community was the sole group that had the political strength and will to impose a solution on Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Europe as you, yourself, said and there was a complex relationship there within Europe, so I don't want to analyse it, but anyway the powers on the European continent did not profess their readiness for Bosnia-Herzegovina and previously for Croatia to use their security, political, and other resources to bring an end to the crisis. And so the fate of all the peace plans was that they failed. Now, when the USA arrived they wielded all the mechanisms, political, diplomatic, military, and probably intelligence and other methods, and the main reason being is that if you look at the territory of the second Yugoslavia or Bosnia-Herzegovina, why the problem couldn't be solved peacefully and why a political solution and peace plans weren't adopted and accepted was the fact that the Serb aggressor -- it didn't suit the Serb aggressor. And most often as had previously been the case in Croatia, they entered into negotiations for tactical reasons, but strategically, and this can be seen specifically on occupied territory, they used the negotiations gradually to neutralise any possible military intervention and finally and ultimately over 70 per cent of the territory was -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina was occupied. It was only after the Washington Accords in 1994 and the different actions on the part of the United States, including - as is said in certain texts and documents publicly accessible - by sending retired officers, and I assume others too, other types too, did full co-operation take place between the BH army, the HVO, and the Croatian army which was reflected in the ultimate outcome, the liberation actions led in 1994 and 1995, and at a point in time when those forces were able to do away with the results of the aggression against B&H, a meeting was -- an agreement was reached. That is to say at the point in time when those forces could resolve the occupation by military means, the negotiation process speeded up once again because it suited certain interests within the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for that answer. One last question. General Praljak testified for almost five months, and very often he mentioned the following, he often talked about the aggression of the Serbs. He always -- often qualified them as aggressors. And I thought I understood when -- that maybe he -- the international community should have been harsher and rougher in dealing with the Serbs who were aggressors. At least that's what I thought I understood, and what he was saying and looking at what he said it might -- you might feel that the international community decided not to intervene, not to do anything, and because there was an aggression underway, the Republic of Croatia and the HVO, the military component of it, did what they had to do in order to face this aggression because no one was intervening to put an end to it. So this was the idea put forth by Mr. Praljak. And could you give us your take on it. Do you believe it's realistic? Is it unrealistic? Is it a true assessment of the situation? Is it completely out of the blue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Basically it's correct. The elements of that are explained here in a scholarly way, in the expert report that is, which speaks about the basic goals of the Serbian armed aggression and their ideological, political, and then ultimately operational outcomes, especially linked to the situation in Serbia at the end of the 1980s, when the first aggression by Slobodan Milosevic and the powers that be were exercised in Serbia first against all the institutions of public and social life. And anybody who didn't want to become part of the project of a future aggression was eliminated. And there are countless -- there is countless evidence of that. Now, the international community did not - and I've written about this -- well, I proclaimed it a breakdown of international security and humanitarian systems because it did not do its job on time, the job that it could have been, and then - and I've also written about this - I think that the international community is not a simple concept nor does it have simple interests nor is it monolithic. It is a conglomerate or a market of different national, multinational, and other interests that exist in today's world. And when the decision was made at the level of the United States and probably some other international powers that we mentioned a moment ago, then the problem was solved by, I would say, the regional forces; that is to say the Republic of Croatia as a state and Bosnia-Herzegovina itself, who then pooled their efforts, they became united, and then from coercion from the international community looking at it objectively and scholarly, it is paradoxical that the victims of a Serb armed aggression which lasted for ten years from 1990 to 2000 including Kosovo, although it was quite clear from the 1990 situation from what was publicly stated where the aggression would go, how it would move and so on and that many parts of the former Yugoslavia were predestined to be victims of an aggression never up until the international community exerted pressure did these victims pool their efforts to resolve the problem. So when it comes to responsibility, we can say that the victims too, in the state of victims states that is, made a mistake and their situation became clearer because they had been completely disarmed and it was quite clear that Serbia would play a hand, play its strongest suit faced with a situation of that kind, which was armed force. Because at that point in time Serbia, in view of the plans to have all Serbs living in one Serb state, it did not suit Serbia to enter into a process of diplomatic or any other peaceful solution to the problem because it was a long, unwieldy process, depending on different mechanisms which can crop up. And the only absolute advantage that they had was in their armed force. And the decision was made as it was made and what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I listened carefully to what you said. You seem to confirm what General Praljak had told us, but if we look at things from this angle, if we believe that the international community was duty-bound to act then there would have been a military conflict with everything we see now in Iraq and Afghanistan occurring. So as far as you're concerned, looking at it from a historical point of view, Croatian point of view, someone who was involved in all these events, according to you, do you think that the international community agreed -- was in agreement to oppose the Serbs or was there a lack of agreement from this international community, a lack of agreement that was known by the Serbs and which the Serbs used to their advantage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already said, the international community was a complex market of different interests, and bearing that fact in mind, Serbia very skillfully dealt with all that on a psychological level and promotional level to a political level using many inherited instruments from the second Yugoslavia, especially its diplomacy because many cadres in the first and second Yugoslavia had their own contacts were -- well, had good contacts. And as I say in my expert report, before 1990 they were not able to prepare themselves in institutional terms for the events that were to follow. And the fact that in all the elections except in Serbia and Montenegro newly established parties came to power is testimony to that. And that only in Montenegro the power was carried on by the structures that had existed previously in Yugoslavia. So that that is one of the facts that had a vital influence on the subject we're discussing here today and, of course, linked to your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mrs. Alaburic, I will give the floor to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction to the transcript. Line 21 it says only that the old structures in Montenegro carried on the structures and the power. The witness said Montenegro and Serbia, so the "Serbia" was left out of the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Perhaps it's not necessary, but out of an abundance of caution, I didn't want to interrupt Mr. Kovacic, but during the last ten or perhaps a bit longer minutes of his direct examination, he asked a number of leading questions which the witness gave general answers. I just want to make sure and I assume that that testimony has no particular evidentiary value beyond what's in the report itself. Either it's documented in the report or it's not. I simply wouldn't want to, a year from now, read references to his testimony as having some value other than what's fully supported in his report. I didn't object. I take it that's the state of the evidence. If it's properly documented in his report it might have some value. The fact that he gave some answers to leading questions in court to similar effect, Your Honour, I would say doesn't add additional weight to his -- that particular evidence. I just wanted to make that clear for the record. While I'm on my feet, Your Honour, I just ask can we leave enough time this evening to inquire about the intentions of other Defence teams so that we can, perhaps, better plan the day tomorrow? I don't know how many other Defence teams intend on asking questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, a particular problem is that Mr. Scott, not objecting at the time, as just referred in a pretty general way now to a number of leading questions. And he's asked for some sort of assurance in relation to the evidential weight of those answers, leaving none of us really knowing where we are. Because if we're talking about a period of 10 or 15 minutes, which answers is he talking about? It really needs to be more specific than that and that is one of the problems. We're not encouraging people to pop up like a Jack-in-a-box all the time, but an objection at the appropriate time would have been helpful in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two topics that have been addressed here, the topic addressed by Mr. Scott and the question you are putting. The Trial Chamber needs to answer your questions, but this question has already been put in the past. Evidence are of two kinds: A, an expert report; and B, questions and answers which the latter provides during the multiple questions put by you, by Defence counsel, and by the Bench. But when a question is leading, the probative value diminishes, of course, compared with a non-leading question. That goes without saying. What does a Bench do when it deliberates? It will look into the specificity of it, will look in the form of the question, and if the Bench realises that the question is a leading question, the Bench can infer that it prompted the question. This is on a case-by-case basis. It's very difficult to say today that this has no value. This is a difficult thing to do. In addition, his testimony is not finished because we haven't heard the questions of the other Defence counsels. There are your questions that need to be put. Now to determine the probative value at this stage is something which seems difficult. It seems to me to be an exploit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: First off, Your Honour, to respond to Mr. Stewart's questions, at least in the past -- in the past 20 minutes, my objection is to all the leading questions. Any lawyer who reads the record knows what a leading question is. When the answer is yes or a generic response was, I saw something to that effect, it's not particularly helpful. It's very clear as to what the nature of the questions and answers were, number one. Number two, Your Honour, again I mentioned on Thursday expectations develop in the course of a three and a half year trial. I had thought it would not be advisable to jump to my feet every time a leading question is asked. However, if I'm now being told that that is the practice, then I will be on my feet and every leading question and every question I think is proper, if that's the way the Chamber wants to proceed. I thought it was improper. I didn't want to interrupt counsel. I thought it would make the point. If I had done so inadequately then I will do it in the future --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Michael, can I just finish off what I got to say, please? Just this once, okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think Mr. Karnavas ought to get the floor now because he's frustrated. Even before you took the floor, he had clearly signalled that he wanted to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to accept that my own frustration should defer to Mr. Karnavas' frustration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We try to distribute frustration equally over everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think it's safer if his has priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I appreciate the courtesy extended to me by Mr. Stewart. I just wanted to say, first and foremost, every attorney whether they're Defence or Prosecution has an obligation to make their record and to make it in a timely fashion, and if not it is waived. They can't close the doors after the horses have run out of the barn. So they can't wait until the end of the testimony and say, Oh by the way, now I want to strike everything. Now what could have been done in this instance, Mr. Scott knows it without having to pop up every time, he could say, I object to any leading question and I have a continuing objection for any further leading question. That preserves his record. It also gives the attorney some indication that perhaps he is leading and to cure the problem. But to allow the attorney to go on, even if he may be experienced, on issues especially where the attorney may believe that these are issues that are of a background nature and not issues that are really critical, I think that is setting a trap for the attorney and then somehow coming and asking for the Trial Chamber to step in and say disregard everything and figure it out by the way. It is the obligation of the attorneys to stand up, object, articulate what the basis of the objection is, and if it's -- if they believe that it's going to be a continuing problem to say I have a continuing objection regarding these sorts of questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, in English we often say age before beauty, but I have no idea where that leaves the priorities between Mr. Karnavas and me, on either account. Your Honour, what I was going to say -- there was that -- so far as leading questions are concerned, yes, Mr. Scott is quite right that most experienced lawyers can recognise most leading questions most of the time, but the numerous debates had in the course of this case indicate that drawing a line, sometimes between what is a leading question and what is not a leading question, is a very serious debate. But, Your Honour, the fundamental point here perhaps is -- and this is -- we suggest the solution that the sort of assurance Mr. Scott seeks as to the evidential weight of answers to questions is one that, bluntly, he really cannot expect. He will have to do what we all have to do. He will have to form his own judgements about the likely weight which may or may not be attached to particular answers and he will then have to pursue his case, his cross-examination, in the light of such judgements as he makes, and that's what we do all the time, Your Honour. That's our job, basically, or one of them -- part of our large job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, you raised another issue a while ago. You wanted to know how the other Defence counsel were going to present the cross-examination. The best would be to ask who is going to take the floor when. We -- the Prosecution has been granted three hours and one hour and a half for all other teams. So you have an hour and a half. We would like to know how this one hour and a half is going to be allocated. I believe my colleague wanted to say something too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That is, indeed, the fact. It was before Ms. Alaburic started speaking, so by ways of frustration, it's not unilaterally down, it's also -- I have a very small question, Mr. Jurcevic, a terminological one. In your studies, have you come across any substantiation and support for the thesis that the term "Herceg-Bosna" is tantamount to Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is that the same? Can it be said that this is the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in essence you could say that it is the same -- or rather, the term "Bosnia and Herzegovina" in its contemporaneous meaning has been in use since the Austro-Hungarian times, since 1858. And from that time on -- for instance, when it comes to the Karadjordjevic dynasty in the time of the first Yugoslavia, in some of their documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm talking about the period 1995, maximum. Between 1990 and 1995, you say they are the same. Have you any support for this? Have you come across any documents where they say "Herceg-Bosna" and where, in fact, what they mean is Bosnia and Herzegovina? Or, of course, vice versa they say "Bosnia and Herzegovina," but they mean Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because both terms have their historical heritage, and that's why I wanted to give you this example that in the time of the first Yugoslavia, even if some official documents of the Serbian dynasty, the other term "Herceg-Bosna" was used for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, you should listen carefully to the question and limit the answer to the limit of the question. And the question is 1990 and 1995 and I asked you whether you could point to such documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm thinking about the minutes from the meetings of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency. And some months ago in order to answer this question for myself I Googled this term and there are various links that you get and you can see scanned books and other documents from this period, 1990 to 1995, where this term is used in public media, discourse, as a substitute term for Bosnia and Herzegovina, just as very often in official documents and discourse in this period, 1990 to 1995, the term "Bosnia" is used to denote Bosnia and Herzegovina and that's incorrect usage. In various international documents, the term "Bosnia" is used rather frequently instead of the correct term "Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me get back to the topic addressed by Mr. Stewart, namely, how the counsel are going to share out that time. Mr. Scott mentioned this also. The best would be to ask each team when they would like to take the floor and how much time they will be taking. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, Mr. President, Your Honours. It is my belief that I will have approximately 15 to as much as 20 minutes, but I believe more in line with the 15. And it was my understanding that the Stojic team was going to go first, but I -- as I understand it they may not have any questions. I don't know. But then after that it was going to be the Petkovic team. So I will follow the Petkovic team. And so if they could reserve 15 minutes for my cross, and I understand from my colleagues they may not have any other questions. So that's -- I think that assists you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. As my learned friend Mr. Karnavas said, our internal organisation is such that Mr. Stojic's Defence would be the first to ask questions but we would like to inform you that we will have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have no questions. Fine. Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to remind you that the request for the cross-examination of this witness were filed only by the Stojic, Prlic, and Petkovic Defence teams, and in your decision of the 7th of May, 2009, that pertained to the motion filed by the Petkovic Defence asking you to review your decision on the right of the cross-examination by Defence teams, you decided that the three teams would have a total of two hours to cross-examine Dr. Jurcevic. And I have to admit that this was the time that we counted on and the Petkovic Defence would like to use the -- all of the time allotted to the Defence and if my colleagues from the other Defence teams would not have any questions, well then I would like to divide that time with Mr. Karnavas as he's indicated. So we anticipate that the Petkovic Defence would use one hour, 45 minutes to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me first check whether you have been granted two hours. I'm sure you're right, but I shall check this out since in my mind it was an hour and a half. So you would be having an hour and 45 minutes and Mr. Karnavas would be having 15 minutes. Let me ask the Coric and Pusic Defence teams whether they have any questions for this witness. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Coric Defence will not have any questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the same goes for the Pusic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic will have one hour and 45 minutes. Mr. Karnavas will have 15 to 20 minutes and he can fill this in. And Mrs. Alaburic will start. This is how the hearing shall unfold tomorrow. That said, we may be getting other documents in the form of binders. The best would be to start tomorrow. Mr. Scott, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thanks. Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, as you know, we will be sitting in the morning tomorrow. We start at 9.00. The witness unit will look after you and escort you into the courtroom. In the meantime, I wish you all a pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
